title: Synchronous Incident Orchestra: Playbook, Bridge Operator Guide, and Status Lexicon
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:
This document defines Redwood's Synchronous Incident Orchestra (SIO) pattern: a prescriptive, low-latency operational model for coordinating cross-functional responders during high-severity incidents. It includes: the Bridge Operator role checklist, a concise signal/status lexicon for internal and customer updates, micro-runbooks for three frequent incident classes (kv-cache storm, GPU throttling/backpressure, model-quality regression), an evidence collection template, an on-call rotation heuristic, and a reusable customer status template set.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: reduce cognitive load during live incidents by standardizing who does what, how we speak internally and externally, and what evidence we collect for postmortem.
- Scope: applies to incidents that trigger a PagerDuty P2/P1 and/or affect Redwood-hosted inference availability, latency SLOs, or model quality affecting customer SLAs. Does not replace service-specific runbooks; it supplements them with orchestration guidance.

Key principles (two-line reminders):
1) Single conductor: the Bridge Operator centralizes messaging, run loop cadence, and decision capture. Do not have multiple people simultaneously authoring customer-facing statuses.
2) Fast evidence, slow narrative: capture telemetry and timelines aggressively; craft the narrative after stabilization.
3) Tiered customer signal: internal severity -> public status -> targeted customer notice (only if impacted).

Roles and responsibilities:
- Bridge Operator (primary): open and operate the incident bridge, own public status cadence, coordinate canary rollbacks/fallbacks, ensure evidence collection. Recommended rotation: on-call SRE or most senior engineer available for first 90 minutes.
- Service Owner(s): subject-matter expert for the failing service (runtime, routing, kv-cache, model infra). Responsible for triage and runbook execution.
- Customer Liaison (CS): drafts targeted customer notices, triggers legal/enterprise comms if necessary.
- Incident Commander (if declared): focuses on high-level decisions (escalate to execs, pause rollouts).
- Observability Lead: owns metric dashboards, traces, SLO delta calculations.

Bridge Operator checklist (first 10 minutes):
1. Acknowledge the page and declare bridge with YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC timestamp.
2. Create incident ticket in tracking system: priority, short summary, affected services, initial hypothesis. Example (curl):
   curl -X POST https://incidents.company/api/v1/tickets -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"summary":"P1: Inference latency spike - us-west-2","priority":"P1","service":"runtime-routing"}'
3. Post short internal Slack channel message (incident-bridge-<id>): one-line impact and link to ticket and status page. Use STATUS LEXICON (below).
4. Assign roles: service owner, observability, customer liaison, and a scribe.
5. Run immediate health checks: service pod counts, 95th/99th latency, error rate, GPU metrics (util, memory errors), KV cache miss rate. Paste outputs to bridge.
6. Decide containment action (throttle, fallback model, regional routing) and execute safe mitigation.

Signal & status lexicon (single-line canonical phrases) for rapid messages:
- INTERNAL: degrading / partial-degradation / outage / performance-regression / quality-regression.
- PUBLIC (status page short form):
  - Operational: no customer impact.
  - Partial degradation: some requests slower or erroring; workaround available.
  - Service outage: customers unable to use endpoint(s).
  - Quality anomaly: model outputs inconsistent with baseline (may not affect availability).
- CUSTOMER NOTICE templates are below (Targeted Notice = TN).

Escalation thresholds (SLO-driven):
- Severity P1 (outage): >= 10% of global requests failing or >99th latency exceed SLO by 200% for >5 minutes.
- Severity P2 (partial degradation): 2–10% customer requests impacted, or 99th latency >150% of SLO for >10 minutes.
- Severity P3: localized/regional noise or single-customer degradation.

Micro-runbooks (quick playbooks intended for Bridge Operator & Service Owner):
1) KV-Cache Storm (symptoms: sudden spike in backend calls, miss_rate >= 20%, tail latency jump)
   - Immediate checks: cache eviction logs, Redis/etcd CPU, network saturations.
   - Quick mitigations (in order):
     a) Enable read-through bypass: route hot prefixes to model runtime with an enforced rate limit.
     b) Scale caching tier (vertical or horizontal) if autoscaler healthy.
     c) Re-enable prefix KVC previews (rolling restart with mem profiling).
   - Rollback criteria: if miss_rate < 5% and tail latency returns within SLO in 15m.
   - Evidence to collect: cache metrics (hit/miss), trace samples showing cache lookup latency, example request ids.

2) GPU Throttle / Backpressure (symptoms: queue buildup, 'cuda OOM' logs, degraded throughput)
   - Immediate checks: node GPU memory, per-process GPU utilization, scheduler queue lengths, host-level I/O.
   - Quick mitigations:
     a) Shift non-critical traffic to lower-priority pool or degraded model variant.
     b) Enable admission control: cap max tokens or per-request concurrency for affected routes.
     c) If hardware fault suspected, cordon node and trigger replacement; if capacity issue, enable burst capacity from Dedicated.
   - Safety note: do not kill model processes without capturing minidumps/traces.
   - Evidence: GPU dmesg, pod logs (OOM traces), scheduler events, admission control metrics.

3) Model Quality Regression (symptoms: increased human-reported failures, eval metric drift, regression alerts)
   - Immediate checks: recent deployments, model rollouts, prompt set failures, eval harness baseline diffs.
   - Quick mitigations:
     a) Rollback to pinned model version or enable deterministic model variant.
     b) Fallback to safety-output filter or apply conservative decoding params.
     c) If rollback infeasible, throttle usage for customers with strict QA.
   - Evidence: prompt/eval set diffs, example model responses, deployment diffs, config changes.

Incident run loop template (recommended cadence):
- T+0m: Bridge open, 10-min triage, containment decision.
- T+10m: Status check, mitigation in-progress, post first public status if customer-impacting.
- T+30m: Stabilization checkpoint; if not stabilized, escalate to Incident Commander.
- T+60m: Decision point: continue mitigations vs. rollbacks vs. declare extended outage and notify execs.
- Recovery: run stabilization 30/60/120 minute updates; after stable for 60 minutes, prepare recovery notice.

Customer status templates (canonical fragments to reduce back-and-forth):
- Short public update (for status page):
  "[HH:MM UTC] Partial degradation: API latency elevated in US-WEST. We have identified increased cache miss rates as a contributing factor and are routing traffic to a fallback path. Engineers are investigating; customers may see higher latency for up to 60 minutes."

- Targeted customer notice (for impacted enterprise customers):
  Subject: [Incident #ID] Brief service impact affecting inference latency
  Body:
  Hi <CustomerName>,
  We observed elevated inference latency impacting <routes>. Our engineers are applying a traffic fallback to reduce error rates while we stabilize the cache layer. Estimated time to full recovery: ~1 hour. We will send updates every 30 minutes or when there is material change.
  - Impact: increased latency, potential timeouts
  - Mitigation in-progress: routing to fallback model, temporarily reducing per-request concurrency
  - Point of contact: <Customer Liaison> (link)

- Recovery notice:
  "[HH:MM UTC] Service recovery: latency back within SLOs. Root cause analysis in progress; postmortem to follow within 72 hours."

Postmortem & evidence checklist (requirements for a publishable RFC-style postmortem):
1) Incident summary (impact, duration, severity).
2) Timeline (minute-granular, who did what). Use the timeline shorthand: [HH:MM] <actor> - <action>.
3) Root cause analysis (1–2 paragraphs) and contributing factors.
4) Evidence artifacts linked: dashboards (direct URLs), logs (selected tsv/csv of error lines), traces (span ids), heapdumps/minidumps, ticket ids.
5) Corrective actions (owner and due date) and preventative actions (monitoring, runbook changes).
6) Customer impact and communication copies.

On-call rotation heuristic (policy, not rigid):
- Principle: minimize cognitive burden for mid-night responders while ensuring senior coverage in business hours.
- Pattern: 7-day primary rotation with a 3-day overlap 'senior-on-call' shadow for high-severity windows (08:00-20:00 local).
- Handovers: automated slack post with recent escalations (last 24h), active incidents, and outstanding action items. Handover must include ticket links and the last three status messages.

Game day (practice) recipe (2–3 hour lab):
- Objectives: validate SIO cadence, test bridge operator handoff, evaluate customer notice creation speed, and measure mean-time-to-first-mitigation (target <15m).
- Participants: 1 Bridge Operator, 2 SREs, 2 Service Owners, 1 Customer Liaison, 1 Observability lead.
- Scenario examples: simulated kv-cache evictions during peak load; model variant rollback during canary.
- Success criteria: attendees complete run loop, evidence artifacts captured, and postmortem written as a learning doc within 48h.

Runbook governance & maintenance:
- Every micro-runbook must be reviewed quarterly by the owning team and validated during at least one game day per year.
- Bridge Operator playbook to be updated after every P1 with a corrective-action that changes language or procedure.

Appendix A — Status page message lexicon (short forms for automated publish):
- OP: operational
- PD: partial_degradation
- OUT: outage
- QRG: quality_regression

Appendix B — Quick evidence command snippets:
- Dump recent 1k logs for service runtime: kubectl -n runtime logs --tail=1000 -l app=runtime > /tmp/runtime-logs-$(date +%s).log
- Capture 99/95 latency: prometheus query: rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="runtime"}[5m]) -> export as CSV via /api/v1/query_range

Appendix C — Minimal postmortem template (copy/paste):
Title: [Incident #ID] <one-line summary>
Severity: P1/P2
Start: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC
End: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC
Impact: <short list>
Timeline:
- [HH:MM] Bridge Operator - opened bridge and created ticket #ID
- [HH:MM] Service Owner - executed mitigation Y
Root cause:
Contributing factors:
Corrective actions:
Preventative actions:
Evidence links:
Customer communications:
Owner(s):
Reviewers:
